- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

1	/-!
2	# ERN — Memory Model v0.2, MM-02 (machine abstraite minimale)
3	
4	Modèle exploratoire de MM-02. Chaque définition et chaque théorème cite la
5	règle MM-02.x qu'il modélise ; le texte des règles reste dans la spécification.
6	Conditions abstraites (par omission) : MM-02.B.4, B.6, B.7 ; MM-02.C.4, C.5, C.6.
7	Hors périmètre : MM-02.1, MM-02.F, MM-02.G.
8	-/
9	
10	namespace Ern.MM02
11	
12	/-- MM-02.5 : autorité d'accès. -/
13	inductive Auth where
14	  | read
15	  | write
16	
17	/-- MM-02.5 : ordre des autorités, `read ≤ write` (réflexif). -/
18	instance : LE Auth := ⟨fun a b => a = .read ∨ b = .write⟩
19	
20	/-- MM-02.3 : octet abstrait, non initialisé ou initialisé avec une valeur
21	d'octet (`val`) et une provenance optionnelle (`prov`, identité d'allocation). -/
22	inductive AByte where
23	  | uninit
24	  | init (val : Nat) (prov : Option Nat)
25	
26	/-- MM-02.2 : allocation abstraite. Son identité est sa clé dans `State.allocs`.
27	`base` adresse de base, `size` étendue, `align` alignement, `live` état
28	d'existence, `bytes` stockage indexé par décalage depuis `base`,
29	`freeAuth` autorité capable de la désallouer, `none` si la désallocation
30	n'est pas applicable. -/
31	structure Alloc where
32	  base : Nat
33	  size : Nat
34	  align : Nat
35	  live : Bool
36	  bytes : Nat → AByte
37	  freeAuth : Option Nat
38	
39	/-- MM-02.4 : emplacement, allocation (`alloc`, identité) et portion de son
40	stockage (`off` décalage, `len` longueur). Interprétation typée et conditions
41	d'accès non modélisées. -/
42	structure Place where
43	  alloc : Nat
44	  off : Nat
45	  len : Nat
46	
47	/-- MM-02.5 : moyen d'accès. `addr` adresse, `prov` provenance (identité
48	d'allocation, v0.1 sans étiquette), `len` plage, `auth` autorité. -/
49	structure Access where
50	  addr : Nat
51	  prov : Nat
52	  len : Nat
53	  auth : Auth
54	
55	/-- État de la machine abstraite : allocations par identité (MM-02.2) et
56	prochaine identité fraîche `next` (MM-02.A). -/
57	structure State where
58	  allocs : Nat → Option Alloc
59	  next : Nat
60	
61	/-- MM-02.A : invariant de fraîcheur, toute identité utilisée est `< next`. -/
62	def WF (s : State) : Prop := ∀ i, s.next ≤ i → s.allocs i = none
63	
64	/-- MM-02.B.2 et MM-02.C.2 : validité spatiale, la plage de l'accès est incluse
65	dans l'étendue de l'allocation. -/
66	def Spatial (a : Alloc) (ac : Access) : Prop :=
67	  a.base ≤ ac.addr ∧ ac.addr + ac.len ≤ a.base + a.size
68	
69	/-- MM-02.B.3 : les `len` octets à partir du décalage `off` sont initialisés. -/
70	def Alloc.InitRange (a : Alloc) (off len : Nat) : Prop :=
71	  ∀ i, i < len → a.bytes (off + i) ≠ .uninit
72	
73	/-- MM-02.B : lecture typée permise. Conditions 1 (stockage vivant),
74	2 (spatial), 3 (initialisation), 5 (autorité de lecture). -/
75	def Read (s : State) (ac : Access) : Prop :=
76	  ∃ a, s.allocs ac.prov = some a ∧ a.live = true ∧ Spatial a ac ∧
77	    a.InitRange (ac.addr - a.base) ac.len ∧ Auth.read ≤ ac.auth
78	
79	/-- MM-02.C : écriture typée permise. Conditions 1 (stockage vivant),
80	2 (spatial), 3 (autorité d'écriture). -/
81	def CanWrite (s : State) (ac : Access) : Prop :=
82	  ∃ a, s.allocs ac.prov = some a ∧ a.live = true ∧ Spatial a ac ∧ Auth.write ≤ ac.auth
83	
84	/-- MM-02.C : effet d'une écriture sur le stockage. Les `len` octets à partir
85	du décalage `off` deviennent `init`, avec `w i = (valeur, provenance)` du
86	i-ème octet écrit ; les autres octets sont inchangés. -/
87	def Alloc.write (a : Alloc) (off len : Nat) (w : Nat → Nat × Option Nat) : Alloc :=
88	  { a with bytes := fun j =>
89	      if off ≤ j ∧ j < off + len then .init (w (j - off)).1 (w (j - off)).2 else a.bytes j }
90	
91	/-- MM-02.C : effet d'une écriture par le moyen d'accès `ac` sur l'état. -/
92	def write (s : State) (ac : Access) (w : Nat → Nat × Option Nat) : State :=
93	  { s with allocs := fun i =>
94	      if i = ac.prov then (s.allocs i).map (fun a => a.write (ac.addr - a.base) ac.len w)
95	      else s.allocs i }
96	
97	/-- MM-02.D : désallocation permise de l'allocation `id` avec l'autorité `auth` :
98	allocation vivante et désallouable (`freeAuth = some d`), autorité compatible
99	selon la relation paramétrique `Compatible`. -/
100	def CanDealloc (Compatible : Nat → Nat → Prop) (s : State) (id auth : Nat) : Prop :=
101	  ∃ a, s.allocs id = some a ∧ a.live = true ∧ ∃ d, a.freeAuth = some d ∧ Compatible auth d
102	
103	/-- MM-02.D : effet d'une désallocation, l'allocation `id` cesse d'exister
104	(état mort) ; son identité reste consommée (MM-02.A). -/
105	def dealloc (s : State) (id : Nat) : State :=
106	  { s with allocs := fun i =>
107	      if i = id then (s.allocs i).map (fun a => { a with live := false }) else s.allocs i }
108	
109	/-- MM-02.2 et MM-02.A : nouvelle allocation sous l'identité fraîche `s.next`,
110	vivante, entièrement non initialisée (MM-02.3). -/
111	def alloc (s : State) (base size align : Nat) (freeAuth : Option Nat) : State :=
112	  { allocs := fun i =>
113	      if i = s.next then
114	        some { base, size, align, live := true, bytes := fun _ => .uninit, freeAuth }
115	      else s.allocs i
116	    next := s.next + 1 }
117	
118	/-- MM-02.E : `ac'` est dérivé de `ac` : sous-plage, même provenance,
119	autorité au plus celle de l'origine. -/
120	def Derive (ac ac' : Access) : Prop :=
121	  ac.addr ≤ ac'.addr ∧ ac'.addr + ac'.len ≤ ac.addr + ac.len ∧
122	    ac'.prov = ac.prov ∧ ac'.auth ≤ ac.auth
123	
124	/-- P1, MM-02.B.1 : toute lecture permise porte sur une allocation vivante. -/
125	theorem read_requires_live {s : State} {ac : Access} (h : Read s ac) :
126	    ∃ a, s.allocs ac.prov = some a ∧ a.live = true :=
127	  let ⟨a, ha, hl, _⟩ := h
128	  ⟨a, ha, hl⟩
129	
130	/-- P2a, MM-02.D : après désallocation de `id`, aucune lecture de provenance
131	`id` n'est permise. -/
132	theorem dealloc_invalidates (s : State) {id : Nat} {ac : Access} (h : ac.prov = id) :
133	    ¬ Read (dealloc s id) ac := by
134	  intro ⟨a, ha, hl, _⟩
135	  simp [dealloc, h] at ha
136	  obtain ⟨b, -, rfl⟩ := ha
137	  simp at hl
138	
139	/-- P2b, MM-02.A : une nouvelle allocation de base `base` quelconque (y compris
140	celle de l'ancienne allocation `id`) ne restaure pas la validité d'un ancien
141	moyen d'accès de provenance `id`. -/
142	theorem reuse_does_not_restore {s : State} (hwf : WF s) {id : Nat} {a : Alloc}
143	    (ha : s.allocs id = some a) {ac : Access} (h : ac.prov = id)
144	    (base size align : Nat) (freeAuth : Option Nat) :
145	    ¬ Read (alloc (dealloc s id) base size align freeAuth) ac := by
146	  intro ⟨b, hb, hl, _⟩
147	  have hne : id ≠ s.next := fun e => by simp [e, hwf _ (Nat.le_refl _)] at ha
148	  simp [alloc, dealloc, h, hne, ha] at hb
149	  subst hb
150	  simp at hl
151	
152	/-- P2c, MM-02.D : après désallocation de `id`, aucune désallocation de `id`
153	n'est permise. -/
154	theorem no_double_free (Compatible : Nat → Nat → Prop) (s : State) (id auth : Nat) :
155	    ¬ CanDealloc Compatible (dealloc s id) id auth := by
156	  intro ⟨a, ha, hl, _⟩
157	  simp [dealloc] at ha
158	  obtain ⟨b, -, rfl⟩ := ha
159	  simp at hl
160	
161	/-- P3, MM-02.C : une écriture permise met à jour les octets de sa plage, qui
162	deviennent initialisés avec les valeurs et provenances écrites. -/
163	theorem write_initializes {s : State} {ac : Access} (hw : CanWrite s ac)
164	    (w : Nat → Nat × Option Nat) :
165	    ∃ a', (write s ac w).allocs ac.prov = some a' ∧
166	      ∀ i, i < ac.len → a'.bytes (ac.addr - a'.base + i) = .init (w i).1 (w i).2 := by
167	  obtain ⟨a, ha, -, -, -⟩ := hw
168	  refine ⟨a.write (ac.addr - a.base) ac.len w, by simp [write, ha], fun i hi => ?_⟩
169	  simp only [Alloc.write]
170	  rw [ite_eq_left ⟨Nat.le_add_right _ _, Nat.add_lt_add_left hi _⟩, Nat.add_sub_cancel_left]
171	
172	/-- P4, MM-02.E : un accès dérivé d'un accès spatialement valide est
173	spatialement valide. -/
174	theorem derive_spatial {ac ac' : Access} (hd : Derive ac ac') {a : Alloc}
175	    (hs : Spatial a ac) : Spatial a ac' := by
176	  obtain ⟨h1, h2, -, -⟩ := hd
177	  obtain ⟨h3, h4⟩ := hs
178	  exact ⟨by omega, by omega⟩
179	
180	/-- P4, MM-02.E : la dérivation préserve la provenance. -/
181	theorem derive_prov {ac ac' : Access} (hd : Derive ac ac') : ac'.prov = ac.prov :=
182	  hd.2.2.1
183	
184	/-- P4, MM-02.E : un accès dérivé n'acquiert pas plus d'autorité que son origine. -/
185	theorem derive_auth_le {ac ac' : Access} (hd : Derive ac ac') : ac'.auth ≤ ac.auth :=
186	  hd.2.2.2
187	
188	/-- MM-02.A : l'identité attribuée par `alloc` (`s.next`) est distincte de toute
189	identité déjà utilisée. -/
190	theorem alloc_fresh {s : State} (hwf : WF s) {i : Nat} {a : Alloc}
191	    (ha : s.allocs i = some a) : i ≠ s.next :=
192	  fun e => by simp [e, hwf _ (Nat.le_refl _)] at ha
193	
194	/-- MM-02.A : `alloc` préserve l'invariant de fraîcheur. -/
195	theorem alloc_wf {s : State} (hwf : WF s) (base size align : Nat) (freeAuth : Option Nat) :
196	    WF (alloc s base size align freeAuth) := by
197	  intro i hi
198	  simp only [alloc] at hi ⊢
199	  have : i ≠ s.next := by omega
200	  simp [this, hwf i (by omega)]
201	
202	/-- MM-02.A : `dealloc` préserve l'invariant de fraîcheur. -/
203	theorem dealloc_wf {s : State} (hwf : WF s) (id : Nat) : WF (dealloc s id) := by
204	  intro i hi
205	  simp [dealloc, hwf i hi]
206	
207	/-- MM-02.A : `write` préserve l'invariant de fraîcheur. -/
208	theorem write_wf {s : State} (hwf : WF s) (ac : Access) (w : Nat → Nat × Option Nat) :
209	    WF (write s ac w) := by
210	  intro i hi
211	  simp [write, hwf i hi]
212	
213	end Ern.MM02

1	# Formalization design
2	
3	Decisions for the Lean formalization. They govern how to formalize, never what ERN means: semantics comes only from `specs/`. Agents follow them. A design question not settled here is proposed in the report, never decided silently.
4	
5	## Goal
6	
7	Check that the spec's rules deliver what ERN promises. A rule that cannot be formalized or proven as written is a result: report it with the failing goal, never work around it.
8	
9	Three results stay distinct: the formal model of the rules, the theorems proven about that model, and later the correctness of the compiler against it. This formalization covers the first two.
10	
11	## Architecture
12	
13	The formalization uses two permanent, complementary models linked
14	by a refinement theorem.
15	
16	This is an architectural decision about formalization, not a
17	normative decision about ERN semantics. Both models must faithfully
18	represent the validated specifications.
19	
20	If a specification cannot be represented faithfully, the mismatch
21	must be reported. Any necessary change to the formalization
22	architecture requires an explicit revision of this document.
23	
24	1. **Abstract model.** Memory is a set of places: variables and field paths (`p.right`). Gives the semantics of safe code. States what safe code may assume about memory.
25	2. **Concrete model.** Memory is byte-addressed allocations. Gives the semantics of safe and unsafe code. Parameterized by a layout interface, never by a fixed layout.
26	3. **Refinement theorem.** Links the two models. It is the formal statement of ERN's safety promise.
27	
28	## Concrete memory
29	
30	- Bytes are abstract: each byte carries its initialization state and, when it belongs to a pointer, its provenance. Address and provenance are distinct.
31	- The concrete model represents every distinction the spec's rules rely on, including storage shared by several places.
32	
33	## Layout interface
34	
35	- Size, alignment and position of each component of a type are abstract functions.
36	- Their guarantees (in bounds, non-overlapping where the spec requires it, aligned) are hypotheses carried as structure fields or typeclass assumptions, never Lean `axiom`s.
37	- The interface contains only guarantees that some spec rule needs. Each hypothesis cites the rule that requires it.
38	- Non-vacuity: whenever the interface changes, a layout satisfying it is exhibited and proven. An unsatisfiable interface would make every refinement result empty.
39	- Realizability for every admissible target and instance is an obligation of the charter's ABI and layout step. It stays recorded as open until that step discharges it.
40	
41	## Main theorems
42	
43	- **Observable behaviors** are defined explicitly: termination with its observable result, trap, undefined behavior, divergence. Refinement compares concrete behaviors projected onto abstract observations.
44	- **Abstract safety.** A program accepted by the static rules has no undefined behavior in the abstract model.
45	- **Refinement.** For every layout satisfying the interface: if each unsafe region satisfies its contract, every observable behavior of an accepted program in the concrete model projects to a behavior of the abstract model. Concrete safety follows from abstract safety.
46	- **Unsafe contracts.** A contract is an entry condition and an exit condition relating the two models. From any state satisfying the entry condition, no execution of the region reaches undefined behavior, and every non-trap exit satisfies the exit condition. A trap is terminal: it runs no cleanup and is compared as an observable behavior. The relation between the models implies the entry condition of any region reachable from safe code; a stronger entry condition must be established by the unsafe code that enters the region. Intermediate states may break the relation, since in sequential execution no other code observes them. Under concurrency, shared state is observable during the region; the contract form for that case is decided before milestone 4.
47	- **Scope.** Every theorem states the language fragment it covers. A theorem on a fragment supports no claim about the whole language; sequential safety implies nothing about concurrent safety.
48	
49	## Construction order
50	
51	1. Control flow infrastructure: abstract syntax and operational semantics of control constructs. No safety theorem yet: the control flow spec's preservation rule depends on the memory and concurrency models.
52	2. Memory model, safe part, on the abstract model. Abstract safety for the sequential fragment.
53	3. Concrete model, layout interface and refinement for the sequential fragment. The memory model counts as verified for that fragment only once refinement is proven.
54	4. Concurrency model: extends both models and the refinement.
55	5. IR dialect, once its dependencies are formalized.
56	
57	The semantic style of milestones 4 and 5 and their target theorems are decided here before they start.
58	
59	## Representation
60	
61	- **Abstract syntax** is built incrementally: only the constructs required by the rules being formalized. No concrete syntax.
62	- **Semantics** is a step function where the spec is deterministic, a step relation where it is not. Interpreters for tests iterate steps with fuel. Running out of fuel is not an outcome, neither termination nor trap. Each interpreter is proven to agree with the unbounded semantics on every result it returns.
63	- **No Mathlib** unless a milestone requires it. Adding it is a design decision recorded here.
64

## MM-02 — Machine abstraite minimale

### MM-02.1 — Valeurs et identité

Dans l'orientation MVS étudiée par ERN, une valeur ne possède pas d'identité intrinsèque.

Une valeur décrit un contenu logique. Son emplacement de stockage peut posséder une identité distincte.

Une valeur peut désigner une ressource possédant sa propre identité, sans que cette identité devienne celle de la valeur.

La copie et le transfert des valeurs sont des opérations distinctes.

L'égalité des valeurs, ses domaines de définition et ses modalités appartiennent au système de types et aux spécifications des opérations concernées.

### MM-02.2 — Allocation abstraite

Une allocation abstraite possède au minimum :

- Une identité unique.
- Un espace d'adressage et une adresse de base abstraite.
- Une étendue.
- Un alignement.
- Un état d'existence.
- Une séquence d'octets abstraits constituant son stockage.
- Une relation avec les autorités capables de la désallouer, lorsque la désallocation est applicable.

Une allocation abstraite représente une unité de stockage dont la validité peut être suivie indépendamment de son emplacement physique.

Elle ne correspond pas nécessairement à un appel d'allocateur dynamique : le modèle doit également pouvoir décrire les stockages automatiques et statiques.

### MM-02.3 — Octets abstraits

Chaque octet abstrait possède un état :

- **Non initialisé.**
- **Initialisé**, avec une valeur d'octet et, lorsque nécessaire, une information de provenance associée.

L'information de provenance doit pouvoir être préservée lors des copies de représentation qui la conservent valablement.

L'état d'initialisation est suivi à une granularité permettant de représenter les allocations partiellement initialisées.

L'initialisation des octets ne suffit pas, à elle seule, à garantir la validité d'une valeur typée.

### MM-02.4 — Emplacements

Un emplacement (*place*) désigne une portion de stockage pouvant contenir une valeur ou un sous-objet.

Il est caractérisé conceptuellement par :

- L'allocation concernée.
- Une portion de son stockage.
- Une interprétation typée lorsqu'elle est applicable.
- Les conditions d'accès pertinentes.

Les emplacements peuvent être composés et projetés en sous-emplacements.

La distinction entre emplacement, valeur et moyen d'accès doit être préservée.

### MM-02.5 — Moyens d'accès et provenance

Un moyen d'accès peut comprendre :

- Une adresse ou une représentation permettant de déterminer l'emplacement désigné.
- Une provenance.
- Une autorité d'accès.
- Des informations supplémentaires nécessaires à la validation de son utilisation.

La provenance permet notamment de distinguer des moyens d'accès associés à des allocations différentes, même lorsque leurs adresses numériques coïncident.

Elle ne se réduit pas nécessairement à l'identité de l'allocation : les règles de permissions et de dérivation peuvent nécessiter des informations supplémentaires.

### MM-02.A — Identité des allocations

Chaque allocation reçoit une identité abstraite distincte.

Une identité d'allocation n'est pas réutilisée pendant une exécution abstraite.

Une adresse peut être réutilisée après la fin d'une allocation.

La réutilisation d'une adresse ne restaure pas la validité d'un ancien moyen d'accès.

### MM-02.B — Lecture typée

Une lecture typée exige :

1. Un stockage vivant.
2. Un accès spatialement valide.
3. Une initialisation suffisante de la représentation requise.
4. Une représentation valide pour le type lu.
5. Une autorité de lecture valide.
6. Le respect des contraintes d'alignement applicables.
7. Le respect des règles de concurrence.

Une lecture typée qui ne satisfait pas une obligation nécessaire à sa sûreté ne peut être exécutée par du code sûr sans vérification ou protection appropriée.

### MM-02.C — Écriture typée

Une écriture typée exige :

1. Un stockage vivant.
2. Un emplacement spatialement valide.
3. Une autorité d'écriture valide.
4. Une valeur admissible pour le type concerné.
5. Le respect des contraintes d'alignement applicables.
6. Le respect des règles de concurrence.

L'écriture met à jour les octets et les états d'initialisation correspondants.

Une écriture peut initialiser un emplacement précédemment non initialisé.

Les effets sur les valeurs ou sous-objets préexistants dépendent des règles de remplacement et de durée de vie qui restent à établir.

### MM-02.D — Désallocation

Une désallocation exige :

- Une allocation vivante et désallouable par l'opération concernée.
- Une autorité compatible avec les conditions de désallocation de cette allocation.
- Le respect des autres invariants nécessaires à la sûreté.

Une désallocation réussie termine la validité du stockage concerné.

Toute tentative d'accès ultérieure à ce stockage par un moyen d'accès invalidé est interdite.

Une opération brute de désallocation qui viole son contrat de sûreté constitue un comportement indéfini.

Une interface sûre peut empêcher cette opération ou produire un échec défini.

### MM-02.E — Dérivation d'accès

Un accès dérivé ne peut acquérir davantage d'autorité que celle autorisée par son origine et par le mécanisme de dérivation.

La dérivation doit préserver les informations nécessaires au contrôle de provenance.

Les règles doivent distinguer la formation d'un moyen d'accès et son utilisation effective.

La simple formation d'une adresse hors limites n'est pas encore classée comme comportement indéfini ; les conditions de validité de son utilisation seront établies séparément.

### MM-02.F — Data races

Une *data race* implique deux accès conflictuels à des portions de mémoire qui se chevauchent, tels que :

- Au moins un accès est une écriture.
- Au moins un accès est non atomique.
- Les accès ne sont pas ordonnés par la relation de synchronisation pertinente.

Une data race constitue un comportement indéfini.

La spécification de concurrence définira les relations d'ordre, les opérations atomiques, les restrictions sur les accès partiellement recouvrants et les mécanismes de synchronisation.

### MM-02.G — Conversions et provenance

ERN doit distinguer :

1. Les modifications d'adresse préservant explicitement une provenance valide.
2. L'extraction de la représentation numérique d'une adresse.
3. La reconstruction d'un moyen d'accès à partir d'une représentation numérique.
4. Les accès à des espaces mémoire externes, notamment MMIO.

Aucune conversion ne doit permettre au code sûr de fabriquer une autorité d'accès invalide.

**Le choix entre provenance stricte, provenance exposée et autres approches n'est pas encore arrêté.**

import Ern.MM02
open Ern.MM02

-- 1. Finder's counterexample: size 0, every byte (incl. ghost) initialized.
def a1 : Alloc :=
  { base := 10, size := 0, align := 1, live := true, bytes := fun _ => .init 7 none, freeAuth := none }
def s1 : State := { allocs := fun i => if i = 0 then some a1 else none, next := 1 }

-- ghost byte exists and carries a value
example : a1.bytes 10 = .init 7 none := rfl
example : a1.bytes 1000 = .init 7 none := rfl

-- yet no read of it is permitted (Spatial fails)
example : ¬ Read s1 { addr := 10, prov := 0, len := 1, auth := .read } := by
  intro ⟨a, ha, _, hs, _⟩
  simp [s1] at ha
  subst ha
  simp [Spatial, a1] at hs

-- 2. General: a permitted read only inspects offsets < size.
theorem read_in_range {s : State} {ac : Access} (h : Read s ac) :
    ∃ a, s.allocs ac.prov = some a ∧ ∀ i, i < ac.len → ac.addr - a.base + i < a.size := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha, -, hs, -, -⟩ := h
  exact ⟨a, ha, fun i hi => by omega⟩

-- 3. General: Read is invariant under arbitrary replacement of ghost bytes.
theorem read_ghost_irrelevant (s : State) (ac : Access) (a : Alloc) (g : Nat → AByte)
    (ha : s.allocs ac.prov = some a) :
    Read { s with allocs := fun i => if i = ac.prov then
             some { a with bytes := fun j => if j < a.size then a.bytes j else g j }
           else s.allocs i } ac ↔ Read s ac := by
  constructor
  · intro ⟨b, hb, hl, hs, hi, hau⟩
    simp at hb
    subst hb
    refine ⟨a, ha, hl, hs, fun i hi' => ?_, hau⟩
    have := hi i hi'
    simp only at this
    have hlt : ac.addr - a.base + i < a.size := by
      obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := hs; omega
    simpa [hlt] using this
  · intro ⟨b, hb, hl, hs, hi, hau⟩
    rw [ha] at hb
    cases hb
    refine ⟨_, by simp, hl, hs, fun i hi' => ?_, hau⟩
    have hlt : ac.addr - b.base + i < b.size := by
      obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := hs; omega
    simp only
    simpa [hlt] using hi i hi'

-- 4. write_initializes's conclusion only names offsets < size (via CanWrite).
theorem write_init_in_range {s : State} {ac : Access} (hw : CanWrite s ac)
    (w : Nat → Nat × Option Nat) :
    ∃ a', (write s ac w).allocs ac.prov = some a' ∧
      ∀ i, i < ac.len → ac.addr - a'.base + i < a'.size := by
  obtain ⟨a, ha, -, hs, -⟩ := hw
  refine ⟨a.write (ac.addr - a.base) ac.len w, by simp [write, ha], fun i hi => ?_⟩
  show ac.addr - a.base + i < a.size
  obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := hs
  omega

-- 5. Nuance: the UNGUARDED effect function can mutate ghost bytes (still unreadable).
example : (a1.write 0 1 (fun _ => (5, none))).bytes 0 = .init 5 none := by
  simp [Alloc.write]
